chapter_text:
CHAPTER 20 — HISTORY OF LIFE ON EARTH

Introduction

How did life begin on the earth, and how did the bewildering variety of living things we see today come into existence? These are among the oldest questions humans have asked. The earth is about 4.6 billion years old, but for its first several hundred million years it was a hostile, lifeless ball of molten and cooling rock. The first simple living cells appeared roughly 3.5 billion years ago, and from those humble beginnings arose bacteria, plants, fungi, animals and, very recently, human beings. This chapter traces two linked stories: (1) how life ORIGINATED from non-living matter, and (2) how, once started, it CHANGED and DIVERSIFIED over enormous spans of time — the process we call EVOLUTION.

20.1 ORIGIN OF LIFE ON EARTH — EARLY THEORIES

Several ideas have been proposed to explain the origin of life.

(a) Theory of Special Creation. The oldest view holds that a divine or supernatural power created all living things in their present form, and that species have remained unchanged ever since. This is a matter of faith and cannot be tested by experiment, so it lies outside the domain of science. Modern biology does not accept special creation as a scientific explanation.

(b) Theory of Spontaneous Generation (Abiogenesis). For more than two thousand years many people believed that living organisms could arise SPONTANEOUSLY from non-living matter — that maggots are born from rotting meat, frogs from mud, and mice from heaps of grain and old rags. This idea is called ABIOGENESIS (life from non-life, happening continuously and easily).

Disproof of spontaneous generation:
 - Francesco REDI (1668) placed meat in jars: some open, some covered with gauze, some sealed. Maggots appeared only in the open jars, where flies could lay eggs. The covered jars had no maggots even though the meat decayed. Redi concluded that maggots come from fly eggs, not from the meat itself.
 - Louis PASTEUR (1864) performed the decisive experiment. He boiled a nutrient broth in SWAN-NECKED (curved-neck) flasks. The curved neck let air in but trapped dust and microbes in the bend, so they could not reach the broth. The sterilised broth remained CLEAR and lifeless for a long time. When the neck was broken or the flask tilted so the broth touched the trapped dust, microbes promptly grew. Pasteur thus proved that micro-organisms come only from pre-existing micro-organisms in the air, and do NOT arise spontaneously. His famous conclusion: 'Omne vivum ex vivo' — all life comes from life.

(c) Theory of Biogenesis. Following Redi and Pasteur, the principle of BIOGENESIS was firmly established: living organisms arise only from other living organisms of the same kind. Biogenesis disproved spontaneous generation, but it raised a new puzzle — if life only comes from life, how did the very FIRST life arise? Biogenesis does not answer this.

20.2 CHEMICAL (OPARIN–HALDANE) THEORY AND THE MILLER–UREY EXPERIMENT

The modern scientific answer comes from the CHEMICAL THEORY of the origin of life, proposed independently by A. I. OPARIN (a Russian scientist, 1924) and J. B. S. HALDANE (a British scientist, 1929). It is also called the theory of CHEMICAL EVOLUTION or the Oparin–Haldane hypothesis.

Main ideas:
 - The early earth's atmosphere was REDUCING (it had no free oxygen). It contained gases such as methane (CH4), ammonia (NH3), hydrogen (H2) and water vapour (H2O).
 - Energy was abundant — from lightning, ultraviolet radiation from the sun, volcanic heat and cosmic rays.
 - Using this energy, the simple gases combined to form simple ORGANIC MOLECULES (amino acids, sugars, fatty acids, nitrogen bases). Rain washed these into the seas.
 - Over millions of years these molecules accumulated in the warm seas, forming a 'PRE-BIOTIC SOUP' (also called the primordial soup or hot dilute soup). They joined into larger molecules — proteins and nucleic acids.
 - These molecules organised into aggregates (Oparin called them COACERVATES) that could grow and divide. Step by step, the first simple living cell — able to reproduce and use energy — finally appeared. Life thus arose from non-living matter, but ONCE only, very slowly, under early-earth conditions that no longer exist (so spontaneous generation does not happen today).

The Miller–Urey experiment (1953). Stanley MILLER and Harold UREY tested the chemical theory in the laboratory. They built a sealed glass apparatus containing the gases of the early atmosphere — methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour. The water was boiled to add vapour and drive circulation, and ELECTRIC SPARKS (simulating lightning) were passed through the gas mixture for about a week. When they analysed the cooled liquid, they found it contained several AMINO ACIDS (such as glycine and alanine) and other simple organic molecules. This was direct experimental support for the Oparin–Haldane idea: the building blocks of life CAN form from simple gases given a suitable energy source.

20.3 EVOLUTION AND ITS MEANING

EVOLUTION is the slow, gradual and continuous change in the inherited characteristics of populations of organisms over many generations, by which new species arise from pre-existing ones. The living world today is the product of about 3.5 billion years of such change. Evolution explains both the UNITY of life (all organisms share a basic cellular chemistry, because all descend from common ancestors) and its DIVERSITY (organisms have diverged as they adapted to different environments).

20.4 EVIDENCE FOR EVOLUTION

We cannot watch the whole history of life directly, but many independent lines of evidence point to it.

(a) Fossils and the fossil record. FOSSILS are the preserved remains, impressions or traces of organisms that lived in the past, usually found in sedimentary rocks. Older rocks lie deeper; the fossils in deeper layers are simpler and older, while those nearer the surface are more complex and recent. Palaeontology (the study of fossils) thus reveals a sequence — life has changed over time. Some fossils are CONNECTING LINKS (transitional forms): Archaeopteryx, for example, had feathers and wings like a bird but teeth, claws and a bony tail like a reptile, linking reptiles to birds.

(b) Comparative anatomy. Comparing the body structures of different organisms reveals relationships.
 - HOMOLOGOUS ORGANS have the SAME basic structure and origin but may perform DIFFERENT functions. Example: the forelimb of a human (arm), a whale (flipper), a bat (wing) and a horse (front leg) all have the same set of bones arranged in the same way. Homologous organs show DIVERGENT evolution from a common ancestor.
 - ANALOGOUS ORGANS perform the SAME function but have DIFFERENT basic structure and origin. Example: the wing of a bird (modified forelimb) and the wing of an insect (an outgrowth of the body wall) both allow flight but are built differently. Analogous organs show CONVERGENT evolution.
 - VESTIGIAL ORGANS are reduced, functionless remnants of organs that were useful in an ancestor. Examples in humans: the vermiform appendix, the muscles that move the ear, the nictitating membrane in the corner of the eye, and the tail bone (coccyx). Their presence shows descent from ancestors in which these organs were functional.

(c) Embryology. The early EMBRYOS of very different vertebrates — fish, frog, reptile, bird, human — look remarkably alike: all show gill-like pouches and a tail at an early stage. This similarity suggests a common ancestry, the differences appearing only later in development.

(d) Molecular evidence. All living things use the same basic molecules — DNA and RNA as genetic material, similar proteins, and the same genetic code. The more closely two organisms are related, the more similar their DNA and proteins are. This biochemical similarity is strong modern evidence for common descent.

20.5 LAMARCK'S THEORY (INHERITANCE OF ACQUIRED CHARACTERS)

Jean-Baptiste LAMARCK (1809) gave the first complete theory of evolution. Its key ideas were:
 - USE AND DISUSE: organs that an animal uses constantly become better developed, while organs that are not used degenerate.
 - INHERITANCE OF ACQUIRED CHARACTERS: characteristics gained by an individual during its lifetime are passed on to its offspring.
His classic example was the giraffe: ancestral giraffes stretched their necks to reach high leaves; the slightly longer neck so acquired was passed to the offspring; over many generations this produced the long-necked giraffe.

Limitations / disproof. Lamarck's theory was rejected because ACQUIRED characters are NOT inherited. Changes in body cells (somatic cells) caused by use, disuse or the environment are not passed to the germ cells (eggs and sperm), so they cannot reach the next generation. August WEISMANN cut off the tails of mice for many generations, yet every new generation was still born with normal tails — showing that an acquired character (a missing tail) is not inherited. A person who builds big muscles by exercise does not have specially muscular children. Only changes in the genetic material (DNA) are passed on.

20.6 DARWIN'S THEORY OF NATURAL SELECTION

Charles DARWIN, after his voyage on HMS Beagle (during which he studied the finches of the Galapagos Islands), published his theory in 'On the Origin of Species' (1859). His theory, often called DARWINISM, rests on a chain of observations and inferences:
 - OVER-PRODUCTION: every species produces far more offspring than can possibly survive.
 - STRUGGLE FOR EXISTENCE: because food, space and other resources are limited, the offspring must compete with one another and with other species and the environment to survive.
 - VARIATION: no two individuals (except identical twins) are exactly alike; individuals within a population vary in size, colour, speed, resistance to disease and so on. These variations are inherited.
 - SURVIVAL OF THE FITTEST (NATURAL SELECTION): in the struggle for existence, individuals with variations that suit them best to their environment have a better chance of surviving and reproducing. Nature thus 'selects' the fitter variants. Their favourable traits become more common in the next generation, while less-fit traits die out.
 - ORIGIN OF SPECIES: over very long periods, the gradual accumulation of favourable variations changes a population so much that a new species is formed.
Darwin's giraffe explanation differs from Lamarck's: the ancestral giraffe population already VARIED — some had longer necks than others by chance. When leaves were high, the longer-necked individuals were better fed, survived and left more offspring; the shorter-necked ones were selected against. Over generations the population became long-necked. The key point is that the variation came FIRST and nature selected from it — Darwin did not claim that stretching lengthened the neck.

20.7 MODERN (NEO-)DARWINISM

Darwin knew that variation and heredity were central to his theory, but in 1859 the mechanism of heredity was unknown. The rediscovery of Mendel's work on genes and the later understanding of MUTATIONS filled this gap. The MODERN or NEO-DARWINIAN theory (the 'synthetic theory') combines Darwin's natural selection with genetics:
 - The raw material of evolution is genetic VARIATION, produced mainly by MUTATIONS (sudden inheritable changes in DNA) and by the reshuffling of genes during sexual reproduction (recombination).
 - NATURAL SELECTION acts on this variation, changing the frequency of genes in a population from one generation to the next.
 - Over time, gene-frequency changes plus reproductive isolation produce new species.
Neo-Darwinism is the framework accepted by biologists today.

20.8 HUMAN EVOLUTION (IN BRIEF)

Human beings (Homo sapiens) evolved from ape-like ancestors over the last few million years. Fossil and molecular evidence shows that humans and the great apes (especially the chimpanzee) share a common ancestor. The broad sequence of human ancestors usually mentioned is: Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus (ape-like forms) -> Australopithecus (walked upright, small brain) -> Homo erectus (made stone tools, used fire) -> Homo sapiens neanderthalensis (Neanderthal man) -> Homo sapiens sapiens (modern humans). The major trends in human evolution were: upright (bipedal) posture, freeing of the hands, a steadily INCREASING BRAIN SIZE, development of language, and the use of tools, fire and culture.

20.9 GEOLOGICAL TIME SCALE (MAJOR ERAS IN BRIEF)

The vast history of the earth is divided into great spans called ERAS, each marked by characteristic life. From oldest to most recent:
 - PROTEROZOIC / pre-Cambrian: origin of the first cells, bacteria and simple soft-bodied life in the seas.
 - PALAEOZOIC ERA ('ancient life'): rise of fishes, amphibians, early reptiles, insects and the first land plants.
 - MESOZOIC ERA ('middle life'): the AGE OF REPTILES — dinosaurs dominated the land; the first birds and mammals also appeared. The dinosaurs became extinct at its end.
 - CENOZOIC ERA ('recent life'): the AGE OF MAMMALS — mammals, birds and flowering plants flourished, and human beings finally appeared. We live in the Cenozoic era today.

SUMMARY

- The earth is ~4.6 billion years old; life appeared about 3.5 billion years ago.
- Early ideas about the origin of life: special creation (faith-based, untestable) and spontaneous generation/abiogenesis (life from non-life), disproved by Redi (maggots from fly eggs) and decisively by Pasteur (swan-necked-flask experiment).
- Biogenesis ('life only from life') replaced spontaneous generation but could not explain the FIRST life.
- The chemical (Oparin–Haldane) theory explains the first life: simple gases of a reducing atmosphere, energised by lightning/UV, formed organic molecules that accumulated as a pre-biotic soup and organised into the first cell. The Miller–Urey experiment produced amino acids from such gases, supporting this.
- Evolution is the gradual change of inherited characters over generations, producing new species.
- Evidence for evolution: fossils (fossil record, connecting links like Archaeopteryx), comparative anatomy (homologous, analogous and vestigial organs), embryology and molecular (DNA/protein) similarities.
- Lamarck proposed inheritance of acquired characters (use and disuse); this was rejected because acquired characters are not inherited (Weismann's mice).
- Darwin's natural selection: over-production, struggle for existence, inherited variation, and survival of the fittest produce new species. Variation comes first; nature selects from it.
- Neo-Darwinism adds genetics: mutations and recombination supply variation, on which natural selection acts.
- Humans evolved from ape-like ancestors with increasing brain size and upright posture.
- The geological time scale divides earth's history into eras: Palaeozoic (fishes/amphibians), Mesozoic (age of reptiles), Cenozoic (age of mammals and humans).

chapter_summary.title: History of Life on Earth — Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This is the NIOS Class 10 Science & Technology (212) Learner's Guide summary for Lesson 20. It traces how life originated from non-living matter on the early earth (the chemical or Oparin-Haldane theory, supported by the Miller-Urey experiment, after spontaneous generation was disproved by Redi and Pasteur), and how living things have changed over time through evolution — covering the evidence for evolution and the theories of Lamarck and Darwin, modern Neo-Darwinism, human evolution and the geological time scale.

worksheet.title: Worksheet — History of Life on Earth (NIOS Official)
worksheet.instructions: This is the NIOS Secondary Science & Technology (212) official Worksheet-20 for Lesson 20. Attempt all questions. Support each answer with named experiments, scientists or examples where relevant.

questions.question: Describe Pasteur's swan-necked-flask experiment. How did it disprove spontaneous generation?
questions.answer: Louis Pasteur (1864) boiled a nutrient broth in flasks with long, curved (swan) necks. The curved neck allowed air to pass freely but trapped dust and air-borne microbes in the bend, so they could not reach the broth. The sterilised broth remained CLEAR and lifeless for a long time. When Pasteur broke off the neck (or tilted the flask so the broth touched the trapped dust), microbes promptly grew. This proved that micro-organisms in the broth come only from pre-existing micro-organisms carried in the air, and do NOT arise spontaneously from the broth. It thus disproved spontaneous generation and supported biogenesis ('Omne vivum ex vivo').
questions.explanation: Air enters but microbes are trapped; broth stays sterile until exposed.

questions.question: State the main ideas of the Oparin-Haldane (chemical) theory of the origin of life.
questions.answer: The chemical theory (Oparin 1924, Haldane 1929) states: (1) the early earth had a REDUCING atmosphere of methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour, with no free oxygen; (2) energy from lightning, UV radiation, volcanic heat and cosmic rays caused these gases to combine into simple ORGANIC MOLECULES (amino acids, sugars, bases); (3) these molecules accumulated in the warm seas as a PRE-BIOTIC ('primordial') soup and joined into larger molecules (proteins, nucleic acids); (4) these organised into aggregates (coacervates) that could grow and divide, eventually giving rise to the first living cell. Life thus arose once, very slowly, from non-living matter under early-earth conditions that no longer exist.
questions.explanation: Reducing atmosphere + energy -> organic molecules -> soup -> first cell.

questions.question: What was the Miller-Urey experiment and what did it prove?
questions.answer: In 1953 Stanley Miller and Harold Urey built a sealed glass apparatus containing the gases of the supposed early atmosphere — methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour. They boiled the water to add vapour and circulate the mixture, and passed ELECTRIC SPARKS (to mimic lightning) through it for about a week. On analysing the cooled liquid they found several AMINO ACIDS (e.g. glycine, alanine) and other simple organic molecules. This proved experimentally that the building blocks of life can form from simple inorganic gases given a suitable energy source, providing strong support for the Oparin-Haldane chemical theory.
questions.explanation: Sparking early-atmosphere gases yielded amino acids.

questions.question: Distinguish between homologous and analogous organs with examples, and state what each indicates about evolution.
questions.answer:
HOMOLOGOUS ORGANS have the SAME basic structure and embryonic origin but may perform DIFFERENT functions. Example: the forelimbs of a human (arm), a whale (flipper), a bat (wing) and a horse (front leg) contain the same set of bones in the same arrangement, though they are used for grasping, swimming, flying and running. Homologous organs arise by DIVERGENT evolution from a common ancestor and show that these animals are related.
ANALOGOUS ORGANS perform the SAME function but have DIFFERENT basic structure and origin. Example: the wing of a bird (a modified forelimb with bones) and the wing of an insect (an outgrowth of the body wall, without bones) both allow flight but are built quite differently. Analogous organs arise by CONVERGENT evolution, where unrelated organisms adapt to a similar way of life.
Thus homologous organs indicate common ancestry (divergent evolution), while analogous organs indicate similar adaptation without close relationship (convergent evolution).
questions.explanation: Same structure/different function vs same function/different structure; divergent vs convergent.

questions.question: State Lamarck's theory and give one reason why it was rejected.
questions.answer:
Lamarck (1809) proposed the theory of INHERITANCE OF ACQUIRED CHARACTERS based on USE AND DISUSE: organs that are used constantly become better developed while unused organs degenerate, and these acquired changes are passed on to the offspring. His example was the giraffe stretching its neck to reach high leaves, the longer neck being inherited over generations.
It was rejected because acquired characters are NOT inherited. Changes in body (somatic) cells caused by use, disuse or the environment do not reach the germ cells, so they cannot be passed to the next generation. Weismann cut off the tails of mice for many generations, yet the offspring were always born with normal tails — proving an acquired character is not inherited.
questions.explanation: Use and disuse + inheritance of acquired characters; rejected as acquired characters are not inherited.

questions.question: Explain Darwin's theory of natural selection using the example of the giraffe.
questions.answer:
Darwin's theory (1859) explains evolution through these points: (1) OVER-PRODUCTION — species produce many more offspring than can survive; (2) STRUGGLE FOR EXISTENCE — limited food and space force individuals to compete; (3) VARIATION — individuals differ in inherited characters; (4) SURVIVAL OF THE FITTEST (NATURAL SELECTION) — individuals whose variations suit the environment survive and reproduce more, passing on those traits; (5) over many generations favourable traits accumulate and a NEW SPECIES forms.
Giraffe example: in the ancestral giraffe population, necks already VARIED in length by chance. When ground vegetation was scarce and food was high up, the longer-necked individuals could feed better, so they survived and left more offspring, while shorter-necked ones were selected against. Generation after generation the average neck length increased, producing the long-necked giraffe. The key idea is that the variation existed first and nature selected the fitter variants — unlike Lamarck, Darwin did not claim that stretching itself lengthened the neck.
questions.explanation: Variation exists first; nature selects the fitter long-necked giraffes.

questions.question: How does Darwin's explanation of evolution differ from Lamarck's?
questions.answer: Lamarck said the ENVIRONMENT directly produces a change in an individual (through use and disuse), and that this acquired change is inherited — so the change comes first and then is passed on. Darwin said inherited VARIATION already exists in a population by chance; the environment does not create it but merely SELECTS the variants that are best suited (natural selection), so the better-adapted individuals survive and reproduce. In short: for Lamarck the trait is acquired during life and then inherited; for Darwin the trait is already inherited and nature selects among existing variants. Lamarck's mechanism (inheritance of acquired characters) was disproved, whereas Darwin's natural selection, strengthened by genetics in Neo-Darwinism, is accepted today.
questions.explanation: Lamarck: acquired then inherited. Darwin: variation pre-exists, nature selects.

questions.question: Name the three major eras of the geological time scale and state the dominant life of each.
questions.answer: (1) PALAEOZOIC ERA ('ancient life') — rise of fishes, amphibians, early reptiles, insects and the first land plants. (2) MESOZOIC ERA ('middle life') — the AGE OF REPTILES, when dinosaurs dominated the land; the first birds and mammals also appeared, and the dinosaurs became extinct at its end. (3) CENOZOIC ERA ('recent life') — the AGE OF MAMMALS, when mammals, birds and flowering plants flourished and human beings appeared. We live in the Cenozoic era today.

questions.question: What are vestigial organs? Give two examples in humans and state what they suggest.
questions.answer: VESTIGIAL ORGANS are reduced, functionless (or much reduced) remnants of organs that were fully developed and useful in an ancestor. Two examples in humans are the VERMIFORM APPENDIX and the TAIL BONE (COCCYX); others include the muscles that move the ear and the nictitating membrane of the eye. Their presence suggests that humans descended from ancestors in which these organs were functional, providing evidence for evolution.
questions.explanation: Functionless remnants (appendix, coccyx) indicate descent from ancestors where they worked.

questions.question: How does Neo-Darwinism improve upon Darwin's original theory?
questions.answer: Darwin's theory explained natural selection but could not say HOW variation arose or how it was inherited, because genetics was unknown in 1859. Neo-Darwinism (the synthetic theory) combines natural selection with modern genetics: it identifies MUTATIONS (sudden inheritable changes in DNA) and the recombination of genes during sexual reproduction as the SOURCES of inherited variation. Natural selection then acts on this genetic variation, changing the frequencies of genes in a population over generations; together with reproductive isolation this leads to new species. Thus Neo-Darwinism supplies the genetic mechanism that Darwin's theory lacked.
questions.explanation: Adds the genetic source of variation (mutation, recombination) that Darwin lacked.

questions.question: The disproved idea that life arises from non-living matter is called ____.
____ used covered and open meat jars to show maggots come from fly eggs.
Pasteur used ____ flasks to disprove spontaneous generation.
The chemical theory of the origin of life was proposed by Oparin and ____.
The early atmosphere lacked free ____.
The accumulation of organic molecules in the early seas is called the pre-biotic or ____ soup.
In the Miller-Urey experiment, ____ sparks were used to mimic lightning.
The Miller-Urey experiment produced simple ____ acids such as glycine.
Preserved remains of past organisms are called ____.
The forelimbs of a human, bat and whale are examples of ____ organs.
Reduced, functionless remnant organs such as the appendix are called ____ organs.
Lamarck's theory is the inheritance of ____ characters.
Darwin's mechanism of evolution is called ____ selection.
A sudden inheritable change in the DNA is called a ____.
The Mesozoic era is called the age of ____.
What is the theory of special creation?
questions.answer: The theory of special creation holds that all living things were created in their present form by a divine or supernatural power, and that species have not changed since. It is based on faith and cannot be tested by experiment, so it is not regarded as a scientific explanation.

questions.question: Describe Redi's experiment and its conclusion.
questions.answer: Francesco Redi (1668) placed meat in jars: some left open, some covered with gauze and some sealed. Maggots appeared only in the OPEN jars, where flies could land and lay eggs; the covered and sealed jars had no maggots even though the meat decayed. Redi concluded that maggots come from eggs laid by flies, not from the meat itself, contradicting spontaneous generation.
questions.explanation: Maggots come from fly eggs, not meat.

questions.question: What does the principle of biogenesis state? What limitation does it have?
questions.answer: Biogenesis states that living organisms arise only from other living organisms of the same kind ('Omne vivum ex vivo'). Its limitation is that, while it correctly disproves spontaneous generation, it cannot explain how the very FIRST living organism arose, since there was no earlier life to give rise to it.
questions.explanation: Life from life; cannot explain the first life.

questions.question: Differentiate between abiogenesis and biogenesis.
questions.answer: ABIOGENESIS (spontaneous generation) is the disproved idea that living things arise readily and repeatedly from non-living matter. BIOGENESIS is the established principle that living things arise only from pre-existing living things of the same kind.
questions.explanation: Life from non-life vs life from life.

questions.question: Describe the conditions on the early earth that allowed the origin of life according to the chemical theory.
questions.answer: According to the chemical theory, the early earth had: (1) a REDUCING ATMOSPHERE containing methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour, with no free oxygen; (2) abundant ENERGY from lightning, ultraviolet radiation, volcanic heat and cosmic rays; (3) warm seas in which organic molecules could accumulate. Under these conditions the simple gases combined into organic molecules that built up into the first cell. These conditions no longer exist today.

questions.question: What is meant by the pre-biotic (primordial) soup?
questions.answer: The pre-biotic or primordial soup is the warm early seas in which simple organic molecules (amino acids, sugars, bases) — formed from atmospheric gases by lightning and UV energy — accumulated over millions of years and joined into larger molecules before life began.
questions.explanation: Where organic molecules concentrated before life.

questions.question: What are coacervates and why are they important in the origin of life?
questions.answer: Coacervates are aggregates (clusters) of organic molecules, named by Oparin, that could take up materials, grow and divide. They are important because they are regarded as precursors of the first living cells — a step between non-living organic molecules and the first true cell.
questions.explanation: Molecular aggregates seen as cell precursors.

questions.question: Why does spontaneous generation not occur today even though life once arose from non-living matter?
questions.answer: Life arose from non-living matter only ONCE, very slowly, under the special conditions of the early earth — a reducing atmosphere with no free oxygen and abundant energy from lightning and UV radiation. Today the atmosphere is oxidising (rich in oxygen), which would destroy delicate organic molecules, and any organic molecules that did form would immediately be consumed by existing organisms. So the early-earth conditions no longer exist, and life does not arise spontaneously now — consistent with Pasteur's finding.
questions.explanation: Conditions differ: oxygen present, existing life consumes molecules.

questions.question: What were the components of the Miller-Urey apparatus and why was each included?
questions.answer: The Miller-Urey apparatus contained: methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour (the gases of the supposed early reducing atmosphere); boiling water (to add water vapour and circulate the mixture, modelling the seas evaporating); and electrodes producing ELECTRIC SPARKS (to simulate lightning as an energy source). A condenser cooled the products into a liquid trap. Together they reproduced early-earth conditions in the laboratory.
questions.explanation: Gases + water + sparks model the early earth.

questions.question: How do the results of the Miller-Urey experiment support the chemical theory?
questions.answer: The chemical theory claims that simple gases of the early atmosphere could form organic building blocks given energy. Miller and Urey sparked exactly such a gas mixture and obtained AMINO ACIDS and other simple organic molecules. This directly shows the proposed first step of the chemical theory is possible, supporting the Oparin-Haldane hypothesis.
questions.explanation: Amino acids really do form from simple gases + energy.

questions.question: The Miller-Urey experiment produced amino acids but not a living cell. Does this weaken the chemical theory? Explain.
questions.answer: No, it does not weaken the theory. The chemical theory proposes that the origin of life happened in many slow steps over millions of years: gases -> simple organic molecules -> larger molecules -> aggregates (coacervates) -> first cell. Miller and Urey demonstrated only the FIRST step (forming amino acids) in about a week. They never expected to make a cell in a flask in days. By showing the first and hardest-to-imagine step is possible, the experiment actually strengthens the theory; the later steps need far longer times and the right environment.
questions.explanation: First step only; full process needs millions of years.

questions.question: Define evolution.
questions.answer: Evolution is the slow, gradual and continuous change in the inherited characteristics of populations of organisms over many generations, by which new species arise from pre-existing ones. It accounts for both the unity and the diversity of living things.
questions.explanation: Gradual inherited change producing new species.

questions.question: How do fossils provide evidence for evolution?
questions.answer: Fossils are the preserved remains or impressions of past organisms, mostly in sedimentary rock laid down in layers. Deeper (older) layers contain simpler, more primitive forms, while shallower (younger) layers contain more complex, recent forms — showing that life has CHANGED over time. Some fossils are connecting links (e.g. Archaeopteryx, between reptiles and birds) that show how one group gave rise to another. The ordered sequence of fossils is strong evidence for evolution.
questions.explanation: Ordered sequence in rock layers + connecting links.

questions.question: What is a connecting link? Give an example.
questions.answer: A connecting link (transitional form) is a fossil or organism that shows features of two different groups, indicating that one group evolved from the other. Example: Archaeopteryx had feathers and wings like a bird but teeth, clawed wings and a bony tail like a reptile, linking reptiles and birds.
questions.explanation: Shows features of two groups; e.g. Archaeopteryx.

questions.question: Distinguish between homologous and analogous organs with one example each.
questions.answer: HOMOLOGOUS ORGANS have the same basic structure and origin but may have different functions — e.g. the forelimbs of a human, bat and whale, built of the same bones but used for grasping, flying and swimming. They show divergent evolution from a common ancestor. ANALOGOUS ORGANS have different structure and origin but the same function — e.g. the wings of a bird and an insect, both used for flight but built differently. They show convergent evolution.
questions.explanation: Same structure/diff function vs diff structure/same function.

questions.question: What are vestigial organs? Give two examples in humans.
questions.answer: Vestigial organs are reduced, functionless (or much reduced) remnants of organs that were well developed and useful in an ancestor. Two examples in humans are the vermiform appendix and the tail bone (coccyx); the ear muscles and nictitating membrane are others.

questions.question: How does embryology provide evidence for evolution?
questions.answer: The early embryos of very different vertebrates — fish, frog, reptile, bird and human — look remarkably alike, all showing gill-like pouches and a tail at an early stage. The differences appear only later in development. This early similarity suggests that these animals share a common ancestor, providing evidence for evolution.
questions.explanation: Similar early vertebrate embryos imply common ancestry.

questions.question: How does molecular biology provide evidence for evolution?
questions.answer: All living organisms use the same basic molecules — DNA and RNA as genetic material, the same genetic code, and similar proteins. Furthermore, the more closely two organisms are related, the more similar their DNA and protein sequences are. This biochemical unity and the graded similarity are strong evidence that all organisms share common ancestors.
questions.explanation: Common DNA/code; closer relatives share more similar molecules.

questions.question: Why are homologous organs said to show divergent evolution while analogous organs show convergent evolution?
questions.answer: Homologous organs share the same basic structure inherited from a COMMON ANCESTOR, but in different descendants they became modified for different functions (arm, wing, flipper). Since the descendants diverged from one ancestral plan, this is DIVERGENT evolution. Analogous organs occur in UNRELATED organisms that independently evolved similar structures because they adapted to a similar function or environment (e.g. flight). Since separate lineages converged on the same solution, this is CONVERGENT evolution.
questions.explanation: Common-ancestor modification vs independent similar adaptation.

questions.question: State the two main principles of Lamarck's theory.
questions.answer: (1) USE AND DISUSE: organs that are used regularly become better developed, while organs that are not used gradually degenerate. (2) INHERITANCE OF ACQUIRED CHARACTERS: characters gained by an individual during its lifetime are passed on to its offspring.
questions.explanation: Use and disuse + inheritance of acquired characters.

questions.question: Explain Lamarck's account of the giraffe's long neck.
questions.answer: Lamarck proposed that the ancestors of the giraffe had short necks but had to stretch them to reach leaves high on trees. Constant stretching (use) lengthened the neck slightly during the animal's lifetime. This acquired longer neck was then inherited by the offspring. Repeated over many generations, this gradual lengthening produced the modern long-necked giraffe.
questions.explanation: Stretching lengthened the neck, which was inherited.

questions.question: Why was Lamarck's theory rejected? Support with an experiment.
questions.answer: Lamarck's theory was rejected because ACQUIRED characters are not inherited. Changes occurring in body (somatic) cells from use, disuse or the environment do not affect the germ cells (eggs and sperm), so they cannot pass to the next generation. August Weismann tested this by cutting off the tails of mice for many successive generations; every new generation was still born with normal tails, showing that the acquired character (a missing tail) was not inherited. Hence Lamarck's mechanism is false.
questions.explanation: Acquired changes don't reach germ cells; Weismann's mice.

questions.question: What is meant by 'inheritance of acquired characters'?
questions.answer: It is Lamarck's idea that characteristics an individual gains during its own lifetime — through the use or disuse of organs or due to the environment — are transmitted to its offspring. This idea has been disproved, since only changes in the genetic material are inherited.

questions.question: State the main postulates of Darwin's theory of natural selection.
questions.answer: Darwin's postulates are: (1) OVER-PRODUCTION — organisms produce far more offspring than can survive; (2) STRUGGLE FOR EXISTENCE — limited resources force competition; (3) VARIATION — individuals vary in inherited characters; (4) SURVIVAL OF THE FITTEST (NATURAL SELECTION) — individuals with favourable variations survive and reproduce more, passing on those traits; (5) over generations this gradually produces NEW SPECIES.
questions.explanation: Over-production, struggle, variation, selection, new species.

questions.question: What is meant by 'struggle for existence'?
questions.answer: The struggle for existence is the competition among organisms for limited resources such as food, space, water and mates. Because far more offspring are produced than the environment can support, individuals must compete with one another, with other species and against environmental conditions to survive.

questions.question: What is meant by 'survival of the fittest'?
questions.answer: 'Survival of the fittest' means that, in the struggle for existence, the individuals best adapted (fittest) to their environment have the greatest chance of surviving and leaving offspring. Here 'fittest' refers to reproductive success, not merely physical strength. Their favourable inherited traits become more common in later generations.

questions.question: Explain how a new species is formed according to Darwin.
questions.answer: According to Darwin, populations contain inherited variations. In the struggle for existence, nature selects the individuals whose variations best suit the environment (survival of the fittest); these reproduce more and pass on their favourable traits. Over very long periods, favourable variations accumulate and the population changes so much — especially if it becomes isolated — that it can no longer interbreed with the original form. A new species has then arisen.
questions.explanation: Accumulated favourable variations + isolation produce a new species.

questions.question: Compare Lamarck's and Darwin's explanations of evolution.
questions.answer: Both Lamarck and Darwin agreed that species CHANGE over time (evolution), but they differed on the mechanism. Lamarck said the environment directly causes a change in an individual through use and disuse, and that this ACQUIRED change is inherited — the trait is gained first, then passed on. Darwin said inherited VARIATION already exists in a population by chance; the environment merely SELECTS the better-adapted variants (natural selection), which survive and reproduce. Lamarck's mechanism was disproved (acquired characters are not inherited), whereas Darwin's natural selection, supported by genetics in Neo-Darwinism, is accepted today.
questions.explanation: Acquired-then-inherited vs pre-existing variation selected by nature.

questions.question: Give a brief account of the main trends in human evolution.
questions.answer: Human beings evolved from ape-like ancestors over the last few million years, sharing a common ancestor with the great apes. The broad sequence is Australopithecus -> Homo erectus -> Homo sapiens. The main trends were: change to an upright (bipedal) posture; freeing of the hands for using and making tools; a steadily INCREASING BRAIN SIZE; development of language; and the use of fire, tools and culture.
questions.explanation: Upright posture, free hands, bigger brain, tools, language.

questions.question: Name the three major eras of the geological time scale in order from oldest to most recent.
questions.answer: From oldest to most recent the three major eras are: the PALAEOZOIC era ('ancient life', the age of fishes and amphibians), the MESOZOIC era ('middle life', the age of reptiles/dinosaurs), and the CENOZOIC era ('recent life', the age of mammals, in which humans appeared).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
For centuries people believed that maggots arose directly from rotting meat. In 1668 Francesco Redi placed meat in three sets of jars: open, gauze-covered, and sealed. Maggots appeared only in the open jars. Nearly two hundred years later, Louis Pasteur boiled broth in swan-necked flasks; the broth stayed clear until the neck was broken.
(a) Which old belief were these scientists testing?
(b) Why did maggots appear only in Redi's open jars?
(c) Why did Pasteur's broth stay clear?
(d) What principle did these experiments establish?
questions.answer:
(a) They were testing the belief in spontaneous generation (abiogenesis) — that life arises from non-living matter.
(b) Only the open jars allowed flies to land and lay eggs on the meat, so maggots (fly larvae) developed there; the covered and sealed jars kept flies out.
(c) The swan neck let air in but trapped dust and air-borne microbes in its bend, so no living microbes reached the sterilised broth, which therefore stayed clear and lifeless.
(d) They established the principle of biogenesis — that living things arise only from pre-existing living things ('Omne vivum ex vivo') — disproving spontaneous generation.
questions.explanation: Both experiments disproved spontaneous generation and established biogenesis.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The early earth had no free oxygen. Its atmosphere contained methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour. Lightning, ultraviolet radiation and volcanic heat supplied energy. Over millions of years, simple organic molecules formed and collected in the warm seas, eventually organising into the first living cell.
(a) What kind of atmosphere is described?
(b) Name two energy sources mentioned.
(c) What is the collection of organic molecules in the seas called?
(d) Which theory does this passage describe and who proposed it?
questions.answer:
(a) A reducing atmosphere (one with no free oxygen).
(b) Any two of: lightning, ultraviolet radiation, volcanic heat.
(c) The pre-biotic or primordial (hot dilute) soup.
(d) It describes the chemical theory of the origin of life (chemical evolution), proposed independently by Oparin and Haldane.
questions.explanation: Reducing atmosphere + energy -> organic molecules -> primordial soup; Oparin-Haldane theory.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
In 1953 Stanley Miller and Harold Urey sealed methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour in a glass apparatus. They boiled the water and passed electric sparks through the gases for a week. On analysing the liquid, they found amino acids and other simple organic molecules.
(a) Why did the scientists use these particular gases?
(b) What did the electric sparks represent?
(c) What did the experiment produce?
(d) Which theory does the experiment support, and why?
questions.answer:
(a) Because they are the gases thought to make up the early earth's reducing atmosphere, so the experiment modelled early-earth conditions.
(b) The electric sparks represented lightning, an energy source on the early earth.
(c) It produced amino acids (such as glycine and alanine) and other simple organic molecules — but not living cells.
(d) It supports the chemical (Oparin-Haldane) theory of the origin of life, because it shows that the organic building blocks of life can form from simple gases given a suitable energy source.
questions.explanation: Models early earth; sparks = lightning; yields amino acids; supports Oparin-Haldane.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The forelimb of a human (arm), a bat (wing) and a whale (flipper) all contain the same set of bones arranged in the same pattern, although they are used for different purposes. In contrast, the wing of a bird and the wing of an insect are built quite differently but both are used for flight.
(a) What name is given to the forelimbs of human, bat and whale?
(b) What name is given to the bird and insect wings?
(c) Which type indicates divergent evolution?
(d) What broad conclusion about evolution do such organs support?
questions.answer:
(a) Homologous organs (same basic structure and origin, different functions).
(b) Analogous organs (different structure and origin, same function).
(c) Homologous organs indicate divergent evolution from a common ancestor (analogous organs indicate convergent evolution).
(d) They support the idea that organisms are related and have evolved — homologous organs from common ancestors, analogous organs by independent adaptation — providing anatomical evidence for evolution.
questions.explanation: Homologous (divergent) vs analogous (convergent); evidence for evolution.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Lamarck explained the giraffe's long neck by saying that its ancestors stretched their necks to reach high leaves, the lengthened neck being passed to offspring. To test such ideas, August Weismann cut off the tails of mice for many generations, yet every generation was born with a normal tail.
(a) What is the name of Lamarck's theory?
(b) According to Lamarck, how did the giraffe get its long neck?
(c) What did Weismann's experiment show?
(d) Why is Lamarck's theory not accepted today?
questions.answer:
(a) The theory of inheritance of acquired characters (based on use and disuse).
(b) Lamarck said the ancestors stretched their necks (use), the slightly longer neck was acquired during life, and this acquired neck was inherited by offspring over generations.
(c) Weismann's experiment showed that an acquired character (the cut-off tail) is NOT inherited — the mice were always born with normal tails.
(d) Because acquired characters are not inherited: changes in body cells do not reach the germ cells, so only genetic (DNA) changes pass to the next generation.
questions.explanation: Inheritance of acquired characters; Weismann disproved it.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A population of beetles varies in colour from light to dark. Birds eat the beetles they can see most easily. On a dark tree bark, the dark beetles are camouflaged while the light ones are easily spotted and eaten. After many generations, most beetles in the population are dark.
(a) What provides the raw material for selection here?
(b) Why do the light beetles decrease in number?
(c) Name the process by which the population becomes mostly dark.
(d) Whose theory does this illustrate?
questions.answer:
(a) The inherited VARIATION in colour among the beetles provides the raw material.
(b) Light beetles are easily seen by birds on dark bark, so more of them are eaten before they can reproduce (they are less fit in that environment).
(c) Natural selection (survival of the fittest) — the better-camouflaged dark beetles survive and reproduce more.
(d) It illustrates Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection.
questions.explanation: Variation + selection by predation -> dark beetles dominate; Darwinian natural selection.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Darwin proposed that nature selects individuals with favourable inherited variations, but in 1859 he did not know how variation arose or how it was inherited. Later, the discovery of genes and mutations explained these. The combined modern theory is called Neo-Darwinism.
(a) What did Darwin's theory not explain?
(b) What is the main source of new heritable variation in Neo-Darwinism?
(c) What does Neo-Darwinism combine?
(d) How does Darwin's view of variation differ from Lamarck's?
questions.answer:
(a) Darwin's theory did not explain how variation arises or how it is inherited, because genetics was unknown in 1859.
(b) Mutations (sudden inheritable changes in DNA), together with the recombination of genes during sexual reproduction.
(c) Neo-Darwinism combines Darwin's natural selection with modern genetics (the source and inheritance of variation).
(d) Darwin held that inherited variation already exists by chance and nature selects among the variants; Lamarck held that the environment directly produces an acquired change which is then inherited.
questions.explanation: Darwin lacked a genetics; Neo-Darwinism adds mutation + recombination.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The history of the earth is divided into great eras. In one era fishes and amphibians rose; in the next, giant reptiles such as dinosaurs dominated the land and the first birds and mammals appeared; in the most recent era, mammals, flowering plants and finally humans flourished.
(a) Name the era of fishes and amphibians.
(b) Name the era of the dinosaurs and what it is called.
(c) Name the most recent era and what it is called.
(d) In which era do we live today?
questions.answer:
(a) The Palaeozoic era.
(b) The Mesozoic era, called the 'age of reptiles'.
(c) The Cenozoic era, called the 'age of mammals'.
(d) We live in the Cenozoic era today.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A student examines fossils dug from a cliff. Fossils in the deepest rock layer are simple shelled sea creatures; higher layers contain fishes, then amphibians, then reptiles, and the topmost layers contain mammals. One fossil, Archaeopteryx, has feathers and wings together with teeth and a bony tail.
(a) Why are the simplest fossils in the deepest layer?
(b) What does the change from lower to upper layers show?
(c) What is special about Archaeopteryx?
(d) What name is given to a fossil like Archaeopteryx?
questions.answer:
(a) Because deeper rock layers were laid down earlier (are older), and the simplest, earliest forms of life lived first.
(b) It shows that life has CHANGED over time, from simple to more complex forms — that is, evolution has occurred.
(c) Archaeopteryx has bird features (feathers, wings) together with reptile features (teeth, clawed wings, bony tail), so it links reptiles and birds.
(d) It is called a connecting link (transitional form).
questions.explanation: Fossil sequence shows evolution; Archaeopteryx is a connecting link.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Humans share a common ancestor with the great apes. Fossils show a series of ancestors: small-brained forms that walked upright, then forms that made stone tools and used fire, leading finally to modern humans. Through this history brain size increased and posture became fully upright.
(a) With which group do humans share a common ancestor?
(b) State two major trends seen in human evolution.
(c) Name the modern human species.
(d) Does sharing a common ancestor with apes mean humans evolved from modern apes? Explain.
questions.answer:
(a) Humans share a common ancestor with the great apes (especially the chimpanzee).
(b) Any two of: change to a fully upright (bipedal) posture; freeing of the hands; steadily increasing brain size; development of language; use of tools and fire.
(c) Homo sapiens (Homo sapiens sapiens).
(d) No. It means humans and modern apes both descended from a SHARED ancestor that lived long ago; humans did not evolve from present-day apes. Modern apes are our evolutionary cousins, not our ancestors.
questions.explanation: Common ancestor with apes; trends: upright posture, bigger brain; not descended from modern apes.
